content: Fetal screening refers to a variety of medical tests that are conducted to evaluate specific traits or characteristics of a developing fetus. Common procedures used in fetal screening include amniocentesis, sonograms, nuchal translucency testing, and genetic screening. The primary purpose of fetal screening is to detect potential birth defects. These tests are often utilized to identify conditions such as Down syndrome, spina bifida, cleft palate, Tay-Sachs disease, sickle cell anemia, thalassemia, cystic fibrosis, and fragile X syndrome. In certain cases, fetal screening is performed to determine whether the pregnancy will be terminated. In other instances, these tests are conducted to identify characteristics of the fetus that are not typically classified as birth defects. In some regions of the world, fetal screening has been used to determine the sex of the fetus, and in cases where the fetus is identified as female, termination of the pregnancy has been reported. The increasing prevalence of designer babies and the ability of parents to select specific traits in their offspring have introduced significant bioethical and legal challenges. These issues are expected to play a central role in debates surrounding reproductive rights throughout the 21st century.
